questions.q: What does std::lock_guard<std::mutex> do that calling m.lock() / m.unlock() manually does not guarantee?
options: It locks the mutex on a separate thread
It automatically unlocks the mutex when it goes out of scope, even if an exception is thrown
It allows multiple threads to hold the lock simultaneously
It converts the mutex into a condition variable
questions.explain: lock_guard is an RAII type: its destructor unlocks the mutex automatically, so an early return or thrown exception between lock and unlock can't leave the mutex permanently locked.

questions.q: Why does std::condition_variable::wait require a std::unique_lock rather than a std::lock_guard?
options: unique_lock is faster at acquiring the mutex
wait() needs to unlock the mutex while sleeping and re-lock it before returning, which lock_guard cannot do
lock_guard cannot be constructed on a std::mutex
Only unique_lock supports RAII
questions.explain: condition_variable::wait must release the mutex while the thread sleeps and reacquire it on wakeup. unique_lock supports unlocking and relocking; lock_guard does not.

questions.q: Why should cv.wait(lk, predicate) be used instead of the no-predicate cv.wait(lk)?
options: The predicate overload runs faster on all platforms
The no-predicate overload is deprecated and removed in C++20
The predicate guards against spurious wakeups and notifications that arrive before waiting begins
The predicate overload does not require a mutex at all
questions.explain: A condition_variable can wake a waiting thread without a real notify_* call (a spurious wakeup), and a notify can also be missed if it arrives too early. The predicate overload re-checks the condition in a loop, handling both cases correctly.

questions.q: In the producer/consumer example, what is notify_one() used for?
options: To unlock the mutex on the producer's behalf
To wake one thread currently waiting on the condition variable
To terminate the consumer thread
To push a new item onto the queue
questions.explain: notify_one() wakes (at most) one thread currently blocked in a wait() call on that condition variable, prompting it to re-check its predicate.

questions.q: What is the main risk of calling mtx.lock() and mtx.unlock() directly instead of using an RAII lock type?
options: The mutex becomes recursive automatically
A thrown exception or early return between lock() and unlock() leaves the mutex locked forever, deadlocking other threads
The compiler will reject the code
It makes the mutex non-copyable
questions.explain: Without RAII, any control-flow path that skips the unlock() call (an exception, an early return) leaves the mutex locked, and every other thread waiting on it blocks forever.
